strengths: Clear, intuitive thesis: The paper connects the breadth of a model's contextual embedding space (representation dispersion, measured via average pairwise cosine distance) to autoregressive predictive performance.

Thorough empirical correlation analysis: The negative correlation between sequence-level / last-token perplexity and representation dispersion is consistently demonstrated across multiple model families (LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, Qwen) and varied domains (WikiText, CNN/DailyMail, PubMed).

Analysis of semantic clusters: Tracking both within-cluster and between-cluster distances across training steps (Figure 7) provides good geometric insight, confirming that representations expand even among semantically related contexts sharing identical continuations.
weaknesses: Artificial setup in label-free downstream prediction (§4.1): The evaluation protocol manually constructs sets with synthetic mixtures of correct and incorrect instances (0% to 100%) and demonstrates a monotonic curve. In practice, a user receives an unpartitioned unlabeled dataset; the paper does not demonstrate how to map an aggregate dispersion value to an accuracy prediction in an absolute, calibrated manner without labeled reference points. Furthermore, while the authors suggest using this to 'inspect only the low-dispersion tail' for error analysis, dispersion is defined as a set-level pairwise statistic (Equation 3), and no instance-level error identification/ranking experiments (e.g., AUROC/F1) are conducted.

Heuristic nature and shift in representations for model selection (§4.2): While Section 3 focuses on contextual sequence representations, Section 4.2 switches to static output projection weights ($W_o$). The dispersion gap metric relies on manually curated sets of domain-specific tokens $T$ (e.g., digits for math, keywords for code), limiting its generality to domains where critical token subsets are not easily isolated a priori.

Narrow evaluation for kNN-LM layer selection (§4.3): The study merely checks the attention vs. FFN sub-layer at the final layer of GPT-2 variants, confirming a known result from Xu et al. (2023) rather than demonstrating that dispersion can reliably select optimal datastore keys across all layers and deeper modern architectures.

Undertrained models in training experiments (§4.4): Training GPT-2 small for only 500 and 1,000 steps leaves the models heavily undertrained (resulting in test perplexities well above 80–150). It remains unverified whether the auxiliary spread-out loss yields benefits at full convergence or translates to improved downstream task performance.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical analysis in Section 3 demonstrating a consistent negative correlation between sequence-level / last-token perplexity and representation dispersion across multiple modern open-weight LLM families (LLaMA, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, Phi) and text domains.
Interesting analysis of semantic clusters in Section 3.3, showing that dispersion expands both within and between clusters sharing the same continuation over training.
The paper is clearly structured and well-illustrated with numerous visualizations across diverse configurations in both the main body and the appendix.
weaknesses: Artificial and flawed evaluation in Section 4.1: The experimental setup creates synthetic mixtures of known correct and incorrect queries using ground-truth labels, which does not validate whether dispersion can predict accuracy on an unseen, arbitrary test dataset. In practice, one does not have labeled partitions to construct these mixtures, and the paper does not show that the dispersion metric correlates with dataset accuracy across diverse held-out benchmarks without ground-truth calibration.

Severely undertrained training experiments in Section 4.4: The push-away training loss is evaluated only on GPT-2 Small trained from scratch for merely 500 to 1,000 steps (achieving perplexities in the 80–200 range). Claiming that this auxiliary loss improves LM pre-training based on such an early, undertrained regime is unsubstantiated; it is unknown whether these gains hold after convergence or scale to standard training budgets.

Superficial evaluation of kNN-LM layer selection in Section 4.3: The experiment only compares the final-layer attention sub-layer against the feed-forward sub-layer on GPT-2, which is already a known phenomenon (Xu et al., 2023). It does not test layer selection across all network layers or report actual downstream retrieval-augmented perplexity to prove that maximizing dispersion systematically finds the optimal layer.

Heuristic nature and limited sample size in Section 4.2: The proposed dispersion gap relies on manually defining task-specific token sets (such as digits or Python keywords) versus generic reference tokens directly on static output embeddings. The evaluation includes very few models per scale (essentially base vs. domain fine-tuned variants), making it hard to disentangle domain-specific vocabulary specialization from general model capability.

Limited theoretical and causal grounding: It is well established in the representation degeneration and logit-lens literature that confident predictions across diverse next tokens require representations to align with separated vocabulary vectors in the un-embedding space. The paper treats dispersion primarily as an empirical phenomenon without formally analyzing how it interacts with prediction entropy, logit scale, or the softmax bottleneck.

strengths: Clear writing, intuitive motivation, and well-structured presentation throughout the manuscript.

Comprehensive empirical investigation in Section 3 demonstrating a consistent negative correlation between sequence/last-token perplexity and representation dispersion across several modern open-source LLM families (Llama 3, Gemma 2, Mistral, Phi-2, Qwen 2.5) and multiple domains.

Insightful analysis of within-cluster vs. between-cluster expansion during training (Section 3.3), demonstrating that dispersion increases even among semantically related contexts sharing identical continuations.
Creative exploration of potential applications, bridging representation geometry to practical workflows including model selection and retrieval-augmented LM layer choice.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty relative to known anisotropy/representation degeneration literature: The phenomenon that contextual embeddings collapse into a narrow cone (anisotropy) and that degenerate representations hurt language modeling is widely documented (e.g., Ethayarajh 2019; Gao et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020). The paper essentially measures the inverse of average cosine similarity, but does not sufficiently contrast dispersion with existing isotropy/intrinsic dimensionality measures.

Methodological limitations in downstream performance prediction (§4.1): The experiment constructs synthetic datasets by mixing known correct and incorrect predictions at varying percentages. Showing that dispersion scales monotonically with this mixture confirms that correct instances have higher dispersion than incorrect ones, but it does not demonstrate how a practitioner can predict absolute downstream accuracy on an unseen, uncalibrated unlabeled dataset.

Severely undertrained models in the training regularization experiments (§4.4): Training GPT-2 Small from scratch for only 500 to 1,000 steps yields test perplexities >80 (far from convergence, where GPT-2 Small typically achieves perplexities <30 on WikiText). Auxiliary losses frequently alter early optimization dynamics without translating into improvements at full convergence; evaluating only at 500–1,000 steps is insufficient to substantiate the claim of improved language modeling performance.

Narrow scope in kNN-LM layer selection (§4.3): The analysis is restricted to comparing only the final attention sub-layer against the final feed-forward sub-layer in GPT-2 variants, primarily echoing observations already documented by Xu et al. (2023) rather than conducting a comprehensive search across all network depths on modern decoder architectures.

Heuristic definition of the dispersion gap for model selection (§4.2): Relying directly on raw output embedding rows for manually curated token sets (digits, Python keywords) is susceptible to confounding factors across architectures, such as embedding dimension, weight-tying schemes, and parameter scaling.

strengths: Extensive and consistent empirical investigation: The paper validates the negative correlation between representation dispersion and perplexity across multiple modern model families (LLaMA, Gemma, Qwen, Mistral, Phi) and distinct text domains.

Comprehensive supplementary evaluation: The appendix provides extensive additional evidence, including validation across training trajectories (OLMo-7B), robustness under metric substitution (Vendi score), multilingual datasets, and calibration experiments.

Creative, practical applications: The paper explores several lightweight, label-free applications, particularly using the dispersion gap over static output embeddings for zero-inference model screening and using layer dispersion as a diagnostic for retrieval keys in kNN-LM.
Clear writing and well-structured presentation: The narrative is easy to follow, the core hypothesis is clearly articulated, and the empirical setup is well-documented.
weaknesses: Unclear mechanism for individual instance hardness ranking: In Section 3.1, dispersion is computed as an average pairwise cosine distance over a set/batch of 100 queries with artificial mixtures of correct/incorrect predictions. It is not made adequately clear how this set-level metric is operationalized to score, rank, or filter individual instances in a real-world unlabeled dataset.

Toy-scale training experiments: The training exploration in Section 3.4 is evaluated exclusively on GPT-2 Small trained from scratch for only 500 to 1,000 steps. Because the model is nowhere near convergence at 1,000 steps (perplexities remain very high, >80), it is unclear whether the 'push-away' objective offers lasting benefits or degrades performance once representations naturally differentiate later in training.

Limited depth in layer selection analysis: Section 3.3 only contrasts the final attention sub-layer against the final feed-forward sub-layer, which largely recapitulates known empirical findings from prior work (Xu et al., 2023). A full layer-by-layer sweep demonstrating that dispersion predicts end-to-end kNN-LM performance across all network depths would make this claim much stronger.

Lack of theoretical grounding: The phenomenon is closely tied to known geometric issues such as representation degeneration, anisotropy, and contrastive uniformity. The paper treats dispersion primarily as an empirical observation without formalizing the mathematical interplay between softmax cross-entropy minimization, logit margins, and latent vector dispersion.

strengths: Extensive empirical analysis demonstrating the negative correlation between perplexity and representation dispersion across multiple modern open-weight model families (LLaMA-3.1/3.2, Gemma-2, Qwen-2.5, Mistral-7B, Phi-2) and diverse corpora (WikiText-103, CNN/DailyMail, PubMed).

Thorough appendix exploring diverse aspects, including metric robustness via Vendi score, layer-wise evolution, within-cluster vs. between-cluster dynamics, and tracking dispersion over the training trajectory of Olmo-7B.

Broad exploration of potential practical applications of representation dispersion, spanning label-free hardness slicing, lightweight model selection, and sub-layer selection for retrieval-augmented models.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: The relationship between representation collapse/anisotropy, uniformity, and representation quality is a well-established theme in representation learning (e.g., Wang & Isola, 2020; Gao et al., 2019; Ethayarajh, 2019). Connecting higher dispersion/uniformity to sharper predictive distributions is conceptually expected.

Artificial setup for hardness estimation (§3.1): The experimental protocol relies on synthetically constructed mixtures of known correct and incorrect items to show batch-level dispersion changes. The paper does not demonstrate a practical, actionable instance-level difficulty ranking or active learning pipeline evaluated against standard uncertainty/confidence baselines (e.g., predictive entropy, token margins).

Heuristic nature of the model selection metric (§3.2): The 'Dispersion Gap' relies on manually defining task-specific token subsets (e.g., digits for math, Python keywords for code) directly on the output projection matrix. The evaluation is limited to a few comparisons within the same family (Qwen vs. Qwen-Math, LLaMA vs. CodeLLaMA), which may be confounded by domain-token frequency shifts rather than generalizable across diverse model families.

Toy-scale training evaluation (§3.4): The auxiliary loss experiments are conducted solely on GPT-2 Small trained from scratch for only 1,000 steps. Training an under-parameterized model for 1,000 steps (where perplexity remains extremely high, >80) is insufficient to establish whether dispersion regularization provides tangible benefits in realistic pre-training or continued pre-training regimes.

Narrow kNN-LM investigation (§3.3): Evaluating only the final layer's Attention vs. FFN sub-layers on GPT-2 replicates known phenomena (e.g., Xu et al., 2023) without examining full layer selection across modern architectures.

strengths: Extensive empirical exploration across multiple contemporary open-weight LLM families (LLaMA-3.x, Gemma-2, Mistral, Qwen-2.5, Phi-2) and domains (WikiText, CNN/DailyMail, PubMed), demonstrating a consistent correlation between sequence-level perplexity and representation dispersion.

The paper explores multiple practical downstream angles beyond pure observation, including label-free slice difficulty assessment, checkpoint screening, layer selection for retrieval-augmented models, and auxiliary training objectives.

Comprehensive appendix containing detailed experimental setups, metric robustness checks (e.g., comparing pairwise cosine distance against the Vendi Score), held-out test evaluations, and checkpoint trajectories across training (Olmo-7B).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty relative to established literature on representation degeneration, anisotropy, and hyperspherical uniformity. Seminal works (e.g., Ethayarajh, 2019; Gao et al., 2019; Wang & Isola, 2020 on uniformity vs. alignment; Jain et al., 2023) have already extensively documented that representation collapse/anisotropy harms LM capacity and that repelling representations improves representations. The paper positions dispersion as a novel discovery rather than grounding it thoroughly in existing uniformity/isotropy frameworks.

Methodological disconnect in 'ranking example hardness' (§3.1): Representation dispersion is defined as a pairwise statistic over a set of embeddings (Eq. 1). In Section 3.1, the evaluation constructs synthetic sets/slices of 100 queries with predetermined correct/incorrect ratios. While this demonstrates slice-level correlation, the paper claims it provides an individual example hardness ranking mechanism without clearly formalizing or evaluating an instance-level score.

Confounding factors in model selection (§3.2): The 'dispersion gap' operates directly on the output projection matrix $W_o$ for domain tokens (e.g., digits, Python keywords). In specialized models (e.g., CodeLlama, Qwen-Math), the output embeddings for domain-specific tokens are heavily updated during domain continual pre-training/fine-tuning. As a result, the dispersion gap likely acts as a simple detector of domain fine-tuning exposure rather than a general indicator of reasoning capacity.

Under-trained models in the training intervention experiments (§3.4): Training GPT-2 Small for only 1,000 steps represents an extremely early checkpoint where the model is far from convergence (test perplexities remain above 80–100). It is well documented that repulsive/entropy-maximizing regularizers accelerate early optimization by preventing premature representational collapse, but there is no evidence that these gains persist at full convergence or scale to larger architectures.

Incomplete validation for kNN-LM layer selection (§3.3): The analysis only verifies that the final layer's attention output is more dispersed than the feed-forward output in GPT-2 variants, echoing findings already reported by Xu et al. (2023). It does not perform an end-to-end evaluation across all layers to demonstrate that dispersion rank order faithfully mirrors end-to-end kNN-LM generation performance.
